ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

> One approach to identifying agent-generated data is to apply exclusion criteria developed for human participants.

> Online participants were recruited through Prolific (https://www.prolific.com), completed the task remotely on their own devices, and received £3 as compensation.

> All lab and online participants gave informed consent before beginning the task, took part voluntarily, and could stop at any time.

> Development of the AEA took place in January 2026, before human data collection, and no data from our participants were provided to the system.

> Participants were instructed to identify the ink color and to ignore the semantic content of the word.

> Each cubicle contained a desktop computer with a monitor, a keyboard, and a mouse; participants were seated approximately 60 cm from the screen.

> Participants read an information letter and provided informed consent.

> Online participants completed an identical copy of the experiment remotely on their own devices, with no supervision and no control over viewing conditions.

> Most existing bot-detection and authenticity checks are built into survey platforms or applied before participants enter a study (CloudResearch, n.d.; Prolific, 2026).

> To our knowledge, as of November 2026, only one sample provider offers checks that run during a study (Prolific, 2026).

> To illustrate this, in October 2026 the first author advertised a study on Prolific that was set up only for this test.

> 4 The AGEA completed the study undetected, without any warning or flag from Prolific.

> No other participants took part, and the reward was paid only to that account.

> Sampling frame Method: Samples Lab: university students; online: Prolific, 51 of 54 drawn; AEA: 51 respondents 3c.

Ethics approval statement:

> The study was approved by the Ethics Review Board of the Faculty of Social and Behavioural Sciences at Utrecht University (reference 26-0757).

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

codebook_check.title: Codebook Check
codebook_check.summary_text:
-  We parsed 59 variable definitions from codebook/README files.
-  16 of 596 data columns (3%) are documented in a codebook; 580 are not.
-  A codebook was found and parsed (59 variable definitions), but its variable names do not match the data columns, so the documentation could not be linked automatically (only 3% of columns matched). For example, the codebook documents ``sample``, ``ex_ID``, ``ID`` while the data has `sample`, `ID`, `orig_ID`. This often means the data holds computed scores or subscales while the codebook lists the underlying items. To make the codebook usable automatically, document variables under the exact names used in the data file (one row per data column), with a label and, for rating items, the response scale.

report: This module checks whether each extracted data column is documented in a codebook or README, and flags documented variables that never appear in the data.
We examined 6 codebook/README/label sources and 596 data columns across 18 files.

**A codebook was found and parsed (59 variable definitions), but its variable names do not match the data columns, so the documentation could not be linked automatically (only 3% of columns matched). For example, the codebook documents ``sample``, ``ex_ID``, ``ID`` while the data has `sample`, `ID`, `orig_ID`. This often means the data holds computed scores or subscales while the codebook lists the underlying items. To make the codebook usable automatically, document variables under the exact names used in the data file (one row per data column), with a label and, for rating items, the response scale.**

#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 18 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: One approach to identifying agent-generated data is to apply exclusion criteria developed for human participants.
Online participants were recruited through Prolific (https://www.prolific.com), completed the task remotely on their own devices, and received £3 as compensation.
All lab and online participants gave informed consent before beginning the task, took part voluntarily, and could stop at any time.
Development of the AEA took place in January 2026, before human data collection, and no data from our participants were provided to the system.
Participants were instructed to identify the ink color and to ignore the semantic content of the word.
Each cubicle contained a desktop computer with a monitor, a keyboard, and a mouse; participants were seated approximately 60 cm from the screen.
Participants read an information letter and provided informed consent.
Online participants completed an identical copy of the experiment remotely on their own devices, with no supervision and no control over viewing conditions.
Most existing bot-detection and authenticity checks are built into survey platforms or applied before participants enter a study (CloudResearch, n.d.; Prolific, 2026).
To our knowledge, as of November 2026, only one sample provider offers checks that run during a study (Prolific, 2026).
To illustrate this, in October 2026 the first author advertised a study on Prolific that was set up only for this test.
4 The AGEA completed the study undetected, without any warning or flag from Prolific.
No other participants took part, and the reward was paid only to that account.
Sampling frame Method: Samples Lab: university students; online: Prolific, 51 of 54 drawn; AEA: 51 respondents 3c.

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 3 R code files.
#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

```{r}
#| echo: false

table <- structure(list(Order = 1:3, File = c("01_data_processing.Rmd", 
"02_quality_and_visual.Rmd", "04_agea_data_processing.Rmd"), 
    "Runs after" = c("—", "01_data_processing.Rmd", "—"), 
    Basis = c("numeric", "dependency", "numeric")), row.names = c(NA, 
-3L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths

**3 data paths in the code do not work in the repository as deposited.** We pointed them to where the file is, so the code could run: `raw_lab.csv` to `data/raw/raw_lab.csv` (in 01_data_processing.Rmd); `raw_online.csv` to `data/raw/raw_online.csv` (in 01_data_processing.Rmd); `raw_aea.csv` to `data/raw/raw_aea.csv` (in 01_data_processing.Rmd). The code should be changed, because as written it does not find these files.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 3 scripts: 0 ran without error, 3 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. text.text: Researchers have long assumed that online behavioral experiments are completed by humans, an assumption AI agents can now violate.
We asked whether agent and human data can be distinguished.
We compared Stroop data from 51 respondents each: humans verified in person, an artificial experiment agent, and an online sample.
All agent-generated respondents showed the congruency effect and passed six quality checks.
A one-class support vector machine (SVM) trained only on human data achieved a median accuracy of 63%.
A supervised SVM trained on human and agent data achieved 94%.
At an assumed 5% contamination rate, most of its flags would be false alarms.
The supervised SVM did not generalize to an agent it was not trained on.
Neither plausible task performance nor the tested SVMs reliably distinguished human from agent data.
These findings suggest that human participation should be safeguarded through study design rather than through screening afterward.

Over the past decade, online recruitment platforms have become increasingly important for social science research, allowing researchers to recruit large and diverse samples quickly (Stewart et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Over the past decade, online recruitment platforms have become increasingly important for social science research, allowing researchers to recruit large and diverse samples quickly <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Stewart et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: More recently, advances in artificial agents based on large language models (LLMs) have raised concerns about the integrity of online research. Westwood (2025) showed that LLM-based synthetic respondents can pass as human participants in online surveys, which may pose an existential threat to online survey research.
text.formatted: More recently, advances in artificial agents based on large language models (LLMs) have raised concerns about the integrity of online research. <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Westwood (2025)</ref> showed that LLM-based synthetic respondents can pass as human participants in online surveys, which may pose an existential threat to online survey research.

text.text: Agents can also complete online behavioral experiments, in some cases with response times and accuracies close to those of humans (Huskey et al., 2026; Özüdoğru, Chetverikov, et al., 2026; Özüdoğru, Van der Stigchel, et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Agents can also complete online behavioral experiments, in some cases with response times and accuracies close to those of humans <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Huskey et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Özüdoğru, Chetverikov, et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Özüdoğru, Van der Stigchel, et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: These studies showed that AI agents can match human data on broad measures, but did not test whether more detailed features could distinguish agent data (data from sessions in which an AI agent completes the experiment) from human data.
Here, we ask whether human and agent data collected in identical versions of a behavioral experiment can be reliably distinguished from the behavioral data alone.
Whether AI agents already threaten online behavioral experiments is contested.

Some researchers have warned that response time studies may already contain agent-generated data (Van der Stigchel et al., 2026); others have argued that task-specific agents are not yet economical to build and that unusual response times are not evidence of bots (Brand et al., 2026; Chetverikov, 2026).
text.formatted: Some researchers have warned that response time studies may already contain agent-generated data <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Van der Stigchel et al., 2026)</ref>; others have argued that task-specific agents are not yet economical to build and that unusual response times are not evidence of bots <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Brand et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Chetverikov, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Still others have countered that once the behavioral markers that distinguish agents from humans are documented, agents can be built to avoid them, so that the markers lose their value for detection (Westwood & Frederick, 2026).
text.formatted: Still others have countered that once the behavioral markers that distinguish agents from humans are documented, agents can be built to avoid them, so that the markers lose their value for detection <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Westwood & Frederick, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: For online surveys, the evidence is more direct: on several platforms, online respondents failed validated AI-detection tests far more often than verified in-person participants, and an agent built with full knowledge of the tests went undetected, although it was slower and costlier to run than a human participant (Zhang et al., 2026).
text.formatted: For online surveys, the evidence is more direct: on several platforms, online respondents failed validated AI-detection tests far more often than verified in-person participants, and an agent built with full knowledge of the tests went undetected, although it was slower and costlier to run than a human participant <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Zhang et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Differences between humans and AI systems in how they process information have been proposed both as architectural limitations of LLMs and as a basis for detecting AI agents.
For example, accuracy losses of LLMs on incongruent Stroop items were interpreted as a lack of executive control (Patel et al., 2026).
text.formatted: For example, accuracy losses of LLMs on incongruent Stroop items were interpreted as a lack of executive control <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Patel et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Cognitive traps based on reported limitations of vision-language models were presented as an effective way to detect agents in online surveys (Affonso, 2026a).
text.formatted: Cognitive traps based on reported limitations of vision-language models were presented as an effective way to detect agents in online surveys <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Affonso, 2026a)</ref>.

text.text: These differences need not be inherent : Patel et al. (2026) also noted that a reasoning model solved the task by writing and executing code, and a public repository of cognitive-trap results suggests that recent models increasingly pass these traps (Affonso, 2026b).
text.formatted: These differences need not be inherent <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">: Patel et al. (2026)</ref> also noted that a reasoning model solved the task by writing and executing code, and a public repository of cognitive-trap results suggests that recent models increasingly pass these traps <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Affonso, 2026b)</ref>.

text.text: Agentic AI systems can overcome limitations of the LLMs they are built on.
They add tools, retrieval, and memory to the LLM and let it direct its own tool use in a loop based on feedback from the environment (Anthropic, 2024).
text.formatted: They add tools, retrieval, and memory to the LLM and let it direct its own tool use in a loop based on feedback from the environment <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Anthropic, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Current commercial agents (e.g., Anthropic, n.d.
; Google, 2025) complete everyday tasks on websites, such as booking a ticket, and can also complete online behavioral experiments.
In a Stroop task, for example, an agent could read the ink color with code instead of resolving the conflict between word and color.
Therefore, poor performance of an LLM in one configuration (e.g., without code execution) neither indicates an inherent limitation nor rules out a threat to online research.
One approach to identifying agent-generated data is to apply exclusion criteria developed for human participants.

In surveys, exclusion criteria are commonly based on attention checks and completion times (Meade & Craig, 2012; Oppenheimer et al., 2009); in response time tasks, on accuracy (e.g., Khng & Lee, 2014; La Pietra & Ruzzoli, 2025).
text.formatted: In surveys, exclusion criteria are commonly based on attention checks and completion times <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Meade & Craig, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Oppenheimer et al., 2009)</ref>; in response time tasks, on accuracy (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Khng & Lee, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">La Pietra & Ruzzoli, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Methods have also been developed to catch the scripted bots of the pre-LLM era, often by looking for random responding (Dupuis et al., 2019; Griffin et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Methods have also been developed to catch the scripted bots of the pre-LLM era, often by looking for random responding <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Dupuis et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Griffin et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: LLM-based agents differ from both, because they complete the task through the same interface as human participants and can produce human-like mean response times and accuracies (Özüdoğru, Chetverikov, et al., 2026; Özüdoğru, Van der Stigchel, et al., 2026).
text.formatted: LLM-based agents differ from both, because they complete the task through the same interface as human participants and can produce human-like mean response times and accuracies <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Özüdoğru, Chetverikov, et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Özüdoğru, Van der Stigchel, et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: However, whether existing checks or detection methods can identify agent-generated data in behavioral experiments has not been tested.
We tested the possibility of identifying agent-generated data with the color-word Stroop task (Stroop, 1935).
text.formatted: We tested the possibility of identifying agent-generated data with the color-word Stroop task <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Stroop, 1935)</ref>.

text.text: The Stroop task is a useful test case because its congruency effect, slower responses when the word and the ink color conflict, is one of the most reliable findings in experimental psychology (MacLeod, 1991; Van Maanen et al., 2009).
text.formatted: The Stroop task is a useful test case because its congruency effect, slower responses when the word and the ink color conflict, is one of the most reliable findings in experimental psychology <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(MacLeod, 1991;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Van Maanen et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: It is also present in most individual participants (Haaf & Rouder, 2019), so its absence may indicate that the participant did not perform the task as intended, and it has been used as an exclusion criterion (e.g., La Pietra & Ruzzoli, 2025).
text.formatted: It is also present in most individual participants <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Haaf & Rouder, 2019)</ref>, so its absence may indicate that the participant did not perform the task as intended, and it has been used as an exclusion criterion (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">La Pietra & Ruzzoli, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: We compared three samples of 51 respondents each (a respondent being one lab or online participant, or one task completion by the artificial experiment agent [AEA]) from the same Stroop task: from humans tested in the lab and verified in person, from the prompt-built AEA, and from an online platform.
We addressed three research questions.
First, would conventional quality checks and visual inspection identify agent-generated data?
Second, how well could machine-learning classifiers distinguish agent from human data when trained on verified human data alone or on labeled data from both humans and agents?
Third, how should the classifiers' output be interpreted for the online data, where it is uncertainfoot_0 whether they came from humans?
text.formatted: Third, how should the classifiers' output be interpreted for the online data, where it is uncertain<ref type="foot" target="#foot_0">foot_0</ref> whether they came from humans?

text.text: Preregistration: No aspects of this study were preregistered.
Materials: The prompts used to develop the AEA and the resulting agent application will be made available to reviewers.
To prevent malicious use, these materials will not be shared publicly.
Researchers may request access from the authors, subject to Utrecht University's nondisclosure agreement.

Data and analysis scripts: All data and scripts required to reproduce the reported analyses, tables, and figures are archived on Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24129387) and available in the GitHub repository (https://github.com/tlhzdgr/AEA), together with a README that explains how to reproduce the analyses and lists the required software and package versions.

text.text: We analyzed data from three samples of 51 respondents each: a lab sample of human participants verified in person, an AEA sample generated by the agent described in the next subsection, and an online sample of participants tested remotely.
Sample size was determined by the feasibility of lab recruitment, and the AEA and online samples were matched to the lab sample in size only.
Because no prior estimate of effect size was available for the classification analyses, no power analysis was conducted.
The lab sample comprised 51 Utrecht University students recruited through the university's recruitment platform.
Eligibility criteria were age (18 years or older), normal or corrected-to-normal vision, and no color blindness.
Participants received 0.5 participation credits.
A researcher, who was present throughout each session (see the Procedure section), verified that the data came from human participants.
Online participants were recruited through Prolific (https://www.prolific.com), completed the task remotely on their own devices, and received £3 as compensation.
text.formatted: Online participants were recruited through Prolific (<ref type="url" target="https://www.prolific.com">https://www.prolific.com</ref>), completed the task remotely on their own devices, and received £3 as compensation.

text.text: Fifty-four respondents completed the task, and none were excluded beforehand.
To match the lab sample size and allow direct comparison between the samples, 51 of these 54 respondents were selected at random, before any quality check was applied.
All lab and online participants gave informed consent before beginning the task, took part voluntarily, and could stop at any time.
All reported being fluent in English.
The study was approved by the Ethics Review Board of the Faculty of Social and Behavioural Sciences at Utrecht University (reference 26-0757).

No procedures to prevent or screen out automated or AI-generated responses were used during data collection, because neither the recruitment platform nor the experiment-hosting platform offered such checks for this experiment; detecting such responses afterward was the subject of this study.
The AEA was developed using Google Antigravity (Google, 2025), an agentic AI development platform, as an extension of the work described in Özüdoğru, Van der Stigchel, et al. (2026).
text.formatted: The AEA was developed using Google Antigravity (Google, 2025), an agentic AI development platform, as an extension of the work described in Özüdoğru, <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Van der Stigchel, et al. (2026)</ref>.

text.text: Development of the AEA took place in January 2026, before human data collection, and no data from our participants were provided to the system.

Throughout the interaction with the development platform, the first author adopted a layperson persona, beginning with one detailed prompt and continuing with conversational follow-up prompts, reflecting how a lay user might naturally interact with a large language model.
The initial prompt gave only the link to the experiment and did not name the task, its conditions, or its expected effects.
It asked the agent to identify the task from the on-screen instructions and to model human response times and accuracy using the available literature on the task.
The AEA was built from natural-language prompts only, and no code was written or edited by the authors.

To reduce the risk of malicious use, further implementation details are withheld from the public description; access arrangements for reviewers and researchers are described in the Research Transparency Statement.
The color-word Stroop task (Stroop, 1935) was implemented in Gorilla Experiment Builder (https://www.gorilla.sc).
text.formatted: The color-word Stroop task <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Stroop, 1935)</ref> was implemented in Gorilla Experiment Builder (<ref type="url" target="https://www.gorilla.sc">https://www.gorilla.sc</ref>).

text.text: Stimuli were the words RED, GREEN, BLUE, and YELLOW and a neutral stimulus XXXX, each presented in one of four ink colors (red, green, blue, or yellow), at a font size of 60 px centered on a white screen.
The task included congruent, incongruent, and neutral trials, in which the word respectively matched the ink color, differed from it, or was XXXX (see Figure 1).
text.formatted: The task included congruent, incongruent, and neutral trials, in which the word respectively matched the ink color, differed from it, or was XXXX (see Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>).

text.text: Participants were instructed to identify the ink color and to ignore the semantic content of the word.
They responded by pressing the standard keyboard keys R, G, B, or Y.
A practice block of 12 trials (four congruent, four incongruent, and four neutral trials) was presented in the same fixed order for all participants.
During practice, feedback followed each response: a green tick for a correct response and a red cross for an incorrect one, each displayed for 400 ms.
The main experiment consisted of 288 trials, 96 per condition, presented in a different random order for each participant.
The trials were divided into three blocks of 96 separated by two self-paced breaks (after trials 96 and 192), which participants ended by pressing the space bar.
The composition of the blocks was not constrained.
Each trial began with a fixation cross presented for 500 ms, followed by the stimulus, which remained on screen until a response was given or for at most 2,000 ms.
If no response was given within 2,000 ms, the message "Too slow!"
was shown for 400 ms and the trial was coded as a miss.
Every trial ended with a 500 ms blank screen before the next trial began.
The structure of the task and a single trial are shown in Figure 1.
text.formatted: The structure of the task and a single trial are shown in Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>.

text.text: The task took approximately 10 minutes to complete. a b Congruent Incongruent Neutral Fixation 500 ms Stimulus ≤ 2,000 ms Blank 500 ms Next trial begins > 2,000 ms 400 ms RED RED XXXX + RED Too slow!

text.text: Note.
Panel a shows example stimuli for the three conditions; panel b shows one trial.
All data were collected between April and May 2026, except the AGEA data (see the Supplemental Material).
Lab sessions took place in individual cubicles at Utrecht University.
Each cubicle contained a desktop computer with a monitor, a keyboard, and a mouse; participants were seated approximately 60 cm from the screen.
Room lighting was dimmed and monitor brightness was held constant across sessions to standardize color perception.
The task ran in a web browser, so the lab computers were connected to the internet.
Participants read an information letter and provided informed consent.
At least one student researcher was present throughout each session.
Online participants completed an identical copy of the experiment remotely on their own devices, with no supervision and no control over viewing conditions.
The AEA completed the task 51 times, one session at a time, on another identical copy of the experiment.
All sessions ran on a personal computer with Windows 11 Enterprise.
Data were processed in R 4.5.2 (R Core Team, 2025).
Each trial of the main experiment was coded as a correct response, an incorrect response (i.e., a key press not matching the ink color), or a miss (i.e., no response before the 2,000 ms deadline).
For all respondents, all 288 main trials were retained, and practice trials were not analyzed.
Task accuracy per respondent was computed as the proportion of correct responses across all trials, with misses counted as incorrect.
Response time measures in the quality checks and the congruency effects were based on correct responses only.
No response time trimming was applied, and no data were excluded at this stage.

We analyzed the data in three steps: (a) we applied conventional quality checks to all data, (b) we tested whether AEA data could be detected with support vector machines, and (c) we applied these detectors to the online sample.
We applied six quality-check criteria to all respondents in all three samples.
Criteria of this kind are commonly used to exclude data in response time studies (Khng & Lee, 2014; La Pietra & Ruzzoli, 2025).
text.formatted: Criteria of this kind are commonly used to exclude data in response time studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Khng & Lee, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">La Pietra & Ruzzoli, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: A respondent was flagged if any of the following was true (a flagged respondent is one that a researcher would usually exclude): (1) task accuracy below .80, (2) mean correct response time below 300 ms, (3) mean correct response time more than 3 standard deviations above or below the mean of its sample, (4) no congruency effect, that is, mean correct response time on incongruent trials no longer than on congruent trials (MacLeod, 1991), (5) more than 10% of trials missed, or (6) fewer than four different response keys used.
text.formatted: A respondent was flagged if any of the following was true (a flagged respondent is one that a researcher would usually exclude): (1) task accuracy below .80, (2) mean correct response time below 300 ms, (3) mean correct response time more than 3 standard deviations above or below the mean of its sample, (4) no congruency effect, that is, mean correct response time on incongruent trials no longer than on congruent trials <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(MacLeod, 1991)</ref>, (5) more than 10% of trials missed, or (6) fewer than four different response keys used.

text.text: The thresholds were set by the authors, based on criteria used in prior work (Khng & Lee, 2014; La Pietra & Ruzzoli, 2025).
text.formatted: The thresholds were set by the authors, based on criteria used in prior work <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Khng & Lee, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">La Pietra & Ruzzoli, 2025</ref>).

text.text: An accuracy below .80 indicates frequent errors in a task with four response options in which most responses should be correct.
A mean correct response time below 300 ms is too fast to be realistic for identifying an ink color and pressing the matching key.
A deviation of more than 3 standard deviations from the sample mean is a common criterion for outliers (Leys et al., 2018).
text.formatted: A deviation of more than 3 standard deviations from the sample mean is a common criterion for outliers <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Leys et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: The congruency effect is one of the most reliable findings in experimental psychology (MacLeod, 1991), so its absence suggests that the task was not performed as instructed.
text.formatted: The congruency effect is one of the most reliable findings in experimental psychology <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(MacLeod, 1991)</ref>, so its absence suggests that the task was not performed as instructed.

text.text: More than 10% missed trials indicates a lack of attention, given the 2,000 ms response deadline, and using fewer than four response keys means that at least one ink color was never reported.
The same thresholds were used for all three samples.
For criterion 3, the mean and standard deviation of the respondents' mean correct response times were computed separately for each sample.
No data were removed because of a quality-check flag.
We also inspected the data visually, as a researcher might do when screening experimental data.
Data from ten respondents, five lab and five AEA, were drawn at random and shuffled.
For each respondent, we plotted the distribution of correct response times, the accuracy per condition, and the congruency effect.
We then tested how well AEA data could be detected from the data alone, in two situations.
In the first, we mimicked a researcher who has only verified human data and tries to detect respondents that differ from them, which is an anomaly detection problem.
For this problem, we applied a one-class SVM (Schölkopf et al., 2001).
text.formatted: For this problem, we applied a one-class SVM <ref type="bibr">(Schölkopf et al., 2001)</ref>.

text.text: In the second, we mimicked a researcher who has also built an agent, as we did with the AEA, and can use its data to train a classifier that tells human and agent data apart.
Here we used a supervised binary SVM to differentiate the classes (Cortes & Vapnik, 1995).
text.formatted: Here we used a supervised binary SVM to differentiate the classes <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Cortes & Vapnik, 1995)</ref>.

text.text: Both classification analyses were run in Python 3.12 with scikit-learn 1.7 (Pedregosa et al., 2011).
text.formatted: Both classification analyses were run in Python 3.12 with scikit-learn 1.7 <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Pedregosa et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: We followed the REFORMS checklist for machine-learning-based science (Kapoor et al., 2024); the completed checklist is given in Table S6 of the Supplemental Material.
text.formatted: We followed the REFORMS checklist for machine-learning-based science <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Kapoor et al., 2024)</ref>; the completed checklist is given in Table <ref type="table">S6</ref> of the Supplemental Material.

text.text: To show which features separated the lab and AEA samples on their own, we also computed the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) for each feature across all 51 lab and 51 AEA respondents, without a classifier.
We report the AUC in whichever direction separated the samples better.
Models.
The one-class SVM (Schölkopf et al., 2001) encodes "normal" data by learning a boundary that encloses most of the training data, here the human lab data only.
text.formatted: The one-class SVM <ref type="bibr">(Schölkopf et al., 2001)</ref> encodes "normal" data by learning a boundary that encloses most of the training data, here the human lab data only.

text.text: New respondents that fall outside this boundary are treated as anomalies.
We counted an anomaly as a flag for possible AEA data.
We used a radial basis function kernel.
The parameter ν is a model setting that, in theory, sets an upper limit on the share of training respondents that fall outside the boundary.
In practice, the share of training respondents flagged can be higher, because respondents that lie on the boundary can also be flagged.
Both ν and the kernel can strongly affect how well a one-class SVM performs, and there are no definite rules for choosing the kernel (Hejazi & Singh, 2013).
text.formatted: Both ν and the kernel can strongly affect how well a one-class SVM performs, and there are no definite rules for choosing the kernel <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Hejazi & Singh, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Without labeled AEA data, which a one-class detector does not use, there is also no clear way to select these settings from the data.
We therefore fixed ν = .08 in advance and used scikit-learn's default kernel width, without tuning either setting.
To test whether this choice affected the results, we repeated the analysis with 1,000 splits for values of ν from .01 to .50.
Median classifier accuracy varied only between .62 and .63 (Table S1 in the Supplemental Material), so our conclusions do not depend on ν within this range.
text.formatted: Median classifier accuracy varied only between .62 and .63 (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">S1</ref> in the Supplemental Material), so our conclusions do not depend on ν within this range.

text.text: The supervised binary SVM was trained on labeled lab and AEA data to separate the two.
It used a radial basis function kernel with scikit-learn's default regularization (C = 1) and kernel width.
For both SVMs, we call a respondent classified as AEA flagged; unlike a quality-check flag, this is a classification, not a judgment of data quality.

To determine classifier performance, we used cross-validation: we split each of the lab and AEA samples at random into a training set and a test set and then combined them, so that every training set and every test set contained equal numbers of lab and AEA respondents.
We repeated this 5,000 times, as suggested for small samples (Monte Carlo cross-validation; Shan, 2022).
In each split, 25 lab and 25 AEA respondents were used for training, and the other 26 lab and 26 AEA respondents for testing.
The one-class SVM was trained on the 25 lab respondents in the training set only, and the supervised binary SVM on all 50.
The features were standardized with the means and standard deviations of each SVM's own training data (lab only for the one-class SVM), and the same values were applied to the test data.
Both SVMs were tested on the same 52 test respondents.
For each split, we computed three measures.

Classifier sensitivity is the share of AEA test respondents that were flagged: sensitivity = true positives true positives + false negatives where true positives are AEA respondents that were flagged and false negatives are AEA respondents that were not flagged.

Specificity is the share of lab test respondents that were not flagged: specificity = true negatives true negatives + false positives where true negatives are lab respondents that were not flagged and false positives are lab respondents that were flagged.
Classifier accuracy is the share of all test respondents classified correctly: accuracy = true positives + true negatives all test respondents
We report the median and the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles across splits.
The percentiles show how much classifier performance varied between splits; they are not confidence intervals.
Means were almost the same as medians.
As a robustness check with more training data, we also ran repeated 10-fold and leave-one-out cross-validation once on all 102 respondents.

These gave similar results for the supervised binary SVM and a somewhat higher classifier accuracy for the one-class SVM (.67), mainly because fewer lab respondents were flagged (Table S2 in the Supplemental Material).
text.formatted: These gave similar results for the supervised binary SVM and a somewhat higher classifier accuracy for the one-class SVM (.67), mainly because fewer lab respondents were flagged (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">S2</ref> in the Supplemental Material).

text.text: To test whether the supervised binary SVM generalized beyond the agent it was trained on, we collected data from 51 respondents generated by a second agent, the artificial general experiment agent (AGEA).

The AGEA was developed by the first author in a separate project to complete behavioral experiments in general rather than the Stroop task alone (Özüdoğru, Chetverikov, et al., 2026), and it completed the same task.
text.formatted: The AGEA was developed by the first author in a separate project to complete behavioral experiments in general rather than the Stroop task alone <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Özüdoğru, Chetverikov, et al., 2026)</ref>, and it completed the same task.

text.text: These data served only as an additional test of the supervised binary SVM; the analysis is reported in the Supplemental Material (Table S5).
text.formatted: These data served only as an additional test of the supervised binary SVM; the analysis is reported in the Supplemental Material (Table <ref type="table">S5</ref>).

text.text: The splits above estimate how well the SVMs perform, but each split used only half of the data for training.

To show how a researcher would apply the method in practice, we refit both SVMs once on all available data: the one-class SVM on all 51 lab respondents and the supervised binary SVM on all 102 lab and AEA respondents, with the features standardized using each SVM's own training data.
We then applied both SVMs to the online sample as an illustration.
The online data were not used for training or evaluation because their composition is unknown.
One online respondent had no correct response on incongruent trials, so its interference could not be computed; the SVMs were therefore applied to the other 50 online respondents.
We report the number and proportion of flagged online respondents with 95% Wilson score confidence intervals (Brown et al., 2001).
text.formatted: We report the number and proportion of flagged online respondents with 95% Wilson score confidence intervals <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Brown et al., 2001)</ref>.

text.text: A flag is only useful if a flagged respondent is likely to be an agent.
This probability, the positive predictive value (PPV), depends on the sensitivity and specificity of a detector and on the proportion π of agent respondents in the sample:
In the cross-validation, classifier performance was determined using test sets in which half of the test respondents were AEA respondents, which is far more than we would expect in a real sample.

Because the composition of the online sample was unknown, we computed the PPV for three assumed contamination rates (5%, 10%, and 20%), using the unrounded median sensitivity and specificity from Table 2.
text.formatted: Because the composition of the online sample was unknown, we computed the PPV for three assumed contamination rates (5%, 10%, and 20%), using the unrounded median sensitivity and specificity from Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">2</ref>.

text.text: These PPV calculations assume that the SVMs would make the same proportion of errors on online data as on the lab and AEA test data, which we could not check without verified online data.
The PPVs in Table 4 use the median sensitivity and specificity; their variation across splits is given in the table note.
text.formatted: The PPVs in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_3">4</ref> use the median sensitivity and specificity; their variation across splits is given in the table note.

text.text: In the Supplemental Material, we also tested whether a more cautious supervised binary SVM, with stricter thresholds or with class weights matching each assumed contamination rate, would make its flags more trustworthy when agents are rare (Table S4).
text.formatted: In the Supplemental Material, we also tested whether a more cautious supervised binary SVM, with stricter thresholds or with class weights matching each assumed contamination rate, would make its flags more trustworthy when agents are rare (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_3">S4</ref>).

text.text: We first asked whether the checks that researchers routinely use would exclude AEA data: common exclusion criteria and visual inspection.
None of the 51 lab respondents and none of the 51 AEA respondents was flagged by any of the six quality-check criteria (Table 1).
text.formatted: None of the 51 lab respondents and none of the 51 AEA respondents was flagged by any of the six quality-check criteria (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>).

text.text: The AEA respondents also stayed well clear of every threshold: their lowest task accuracy was .92, their fastest mean correct response time was 584 ms, no AEA respondent had more than 3 misses in 288 trials, and every AEA respondent showed a congruency effect of at least 113 ms.
Conventional screening would therefore have excluded no AEA respondents.
From the online sample, a single respondent was flagged: its task accuracy was .65, and it had no correct response on incongruent trials, so its congruency effect could not be computed.
Because the online data were collected without in-person verification, we cannot determine whether this respondent was a human or an agent.
Exclusion criteria check each threshold separately, but researchers also look at the data as a whole.

Figure 2 shows the ten respondents: panel a shows the distribution of correct response times and the accuracy per condition (the proportion of correct responses among the 96 trials of each condition), and panel b shows the congruency effect.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">2</ref> shows the ten respondents: panel a shows the distribution of correct response times and the accuracy per condition (the proportion of correct responses among the 96 trials of each condition), and panel b shows the congruency effect.

text.text: Readers can test themselves by trying to identify the AEA respondents before checking the answer in the footnote.
Both groups showed right-skewed response time distributions, high accuracy, and a positive congruency effect, and this held for all 51 lab and all 51 AEA respondents.

None of the AEA respondents showed a pattern that would have typically led to exclusion based on visual inspection, although the AEA respondents had more skewed distributions and larger congruency effects on average, mainly because of larger facilitation (Table S3 in the

text.text: From Human Data?
We next asked whether AEA data can be detected from the data alone.
We used two SVMs for two situations a researcher might face: a one-class SVM trained only on verified human data, and a supervised binary SVM trained on labeled human and agent data.
Both used eight input features and were tested on held-out data across 5,000 random splits.
Table 2 and Figure 3 summarize the performance of both SVMs on the test respondents across the 5,000 splits.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">2</ref> and Figure <ref type="figure">3</ref> summarize the performance of both SVMs on the test respondents across the 5,000 splits.

text.text: With only verified human data, the one-class SVM performed poorly (median classifier accuracy = .63).

It flagged nearly all AEA test respondents (sensitivity = .88) but also about three in five lab test respondents (specificity = .38); the middle 95% of its accuracies across splits lay between .50 and .75, so in some splits it performed no better than chance.

With labeled AEA data, the supervised binary SVM reached a median classifier accuracy of .94 (mean = .93): it flagged nearly all AEA test respondents (sensitivity = .96) and wrongly flagged about one in eight lab test respondents (specificity = .88).
Detection was therefore much better when labeled AEA data were available, but some lab respondents were still flagged.

On their own, the best single features were facilitation (AUC = .91), response time skewness (.90), and response time autocorrelation (.84), whereas task accuracy separated the samples poorly (.60; Table S3 in the Supplemental Material).
text.formatted: On their own, the best single features were facilitation (AUC = .91), response time skewness (.90), and response time autocorrelation (.84), whereas task accuracy separated the samples poorly (.60; Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">S3</ref> in the Supplemental Material).

text.text: A supervised SVM is useful only if it generalizes, that is, if it also correctly classifies respondents from an agent that it was not trained on.

We therefore tested the performance of the supervised binary SVM on data from a second agent, the AGEA, which was designed to complete behavioral experiments in general (Özüdoğru, Chetverikov, et al., 2026).
text.formatted: We therefore tested the performance of the supervised binary SVM on data from a second agent, the AGEA, which was designed to complete behavioral experiments in general <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Özüdoğru, Chetverikov, et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The supervised SVM did not generalize at its default decision threshold: trained on AEA data, it flagged 19% of the AGEA respondents, and its balanced accuracy dropped from .94 to .54.
Conversely, when trained on the AGEA data, a supervised SVM flagged 35% of the AEA respondents, with its balanced accuracy dropping from .96 to .67 (Table S5 in the Supplemental Material).
text.formatted: Conversely, when trained on the AGEA data, a supervised SVM flagged 35% of the AEA respondents, with its balanced accuracy dropping from .96 to .67 (Table <ref type="table">S5</ref> in the Supplemental Material).

text.text: An SVM trained on data from one agent therefore did not detect respondents of an agent it had not been trained on.
Finally, we asked how flags from both SVMs should be interpreted in an online study, where the share of agents or simpler bots is unknown.
We refit both SVMs on all lab and AEA data and applied them to the online sample of 50 classifiable respondents.
Recall that all 50 classifiable online respondents had passed the quality checks; the one respondent that failed them could not be classified.
Because the composition of this online sample is unknown, we have no ground truth to interpret the flags; flagged online respondents therefore did not necessarily come from agents.
The two SVMs differed in how many of the online respondents they flagged (Table 3).
text.formatted: The two SVMs differed in how many of the online respondents they flagged (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">3</ref>).

text.text: The one-class SVM flagged 22 respondents (.44).

If all 50 online respondents were human, the SVM's false-alarm rate for lab data would produce about 21 false alarms when it was trained on 50 lab respondents (leave-one-out, .41) and about 31 when it was trained on 25 (main splits, .62).
The 22 flags are within this range, so they cannot separate agents from humans.
Because the one-class SVM flags anomalies compared with the lab data, its flags may also reflect differences between remote and lab testing, such as devices and testing environments.
The supervised binary SVM flagged five online respondents (.10).

With its false-alarm rate for lab data (.10 in leave-one-out, .12 in the main splits), about five to six false alarms would be expected if all 50 online respondents were human, so these five flags do not by themselves indicate agent participation.
Two online respondents were flagged by both SVMs.

We again emphasize that we could not verify whether the online respondents were human and that these flags should therefore not be read as evidence of agent contamination in this sample.  (Brown et al., 2001).

text.formatted: Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_3">4</ref> shows the PPV at the three assumed contamination rates.

text.text: The one-class SVM's PPV was only slightly higher than the assumed contamination rate in each scenario (.07, .14, and .26 at 5%, 10%, and 20%), so even at 20% contamination about three in four of its flags would be false alarms.
The supervised SVM did better, but its PPV was still low when agents were rare.
At 5% contamination, it was .30: about three in ten flagged respondents would truly be agents, and seven in ten would be false alarms.
Even at 20% contamination, about one in three flags would be a false alarm.

More cautious settings, that is, stricter thresholds (higher cut-offs, so the SVM needs more evidence before flagging a respondent) or class weights matching a low contamination rate, reduced false alarms, on average, only by missing more AEA respondents (Table S4 in the Supplemental Material).

Several studies have shown that AI agents can complete online surveys (Westwood, 2025; Zhang et al., 2026) and online behavioral experiments, in some cases with human-like response times and accuracies (Huskey et al., 2026; Özüdoğru, Chetverikov, et al., 2026; Özüdoğru, Van der Stigchel, et al., 2026).

text.text: Can AEA respondents still be detected from their data alone?
Our results show that the AEA respondents passed all conventional quality checks and looked plausible on visual inspection next to lab respondents.

A one-class SVM trained only on lab data performed poorly at detecting AEA respondents, and a supervised binary SVM trained on labeled AEA and lab data performed well but still flagged some lab respondents.
In practice, having only verified human data is the more realistic situation, because labeled agent data are rarely available for online samples.
Our one-class SVM used only such data but incorrectly flagged about three in five of the lab test respondents.
Several features separated the lab and AEA samples on average, but their distributions overlapped, so some AEA respondents closely resembled lab respondents (Table S3).
text.formatted: Several features separated the lab and AEA samples on average, but their distributions overlapped, so some AEA respondents closely resembled lab respondents (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">S3</ref>).

text.text: For the one-class SVM, the limit therefore lies in this overlap, not only in the choice of classifier.
The supervised SVM reached high classifier accuracy in a balanced evaluation, but its practical value depends on more than accuracy.

When agents are rare in a sample, even a small false-alarm rate produces many false alarms: at an assumed contamination rate of 5%, most respondents flagged as agents would actually be human, if the observed error rates held.
More cautious settings did not solve this problem: on average, they reduced false alarms only by missing more AEA respondents.
The online sample illustrates these false alarms: both SVMs flagged about as many respondents as their false-alarm rates would predict if all respondents were human.
Neither set of flags therefore estimates contamination, and respondents that were not flagged cannot be certified as human.
Automatically excluding flagged respondents could remove much valid data and introduce bias if errors affected some groups of participants more than others.
Two further constraints limit supervised detection in practice.
First, researchers cannot be expected to build an agent, collect data with it, and train a classifier before every online study.

Second, although building such an agent becomes easier as models improve (see Özüdoğru, Chetverikov, et al., 2026), nothing guarantees that a researcher's agent resembles the agents used by fraudulent participants.
text.formatted: Second, although building such an agent becomes easier as models improve (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Özüdoğru, Chetverikov, et al., 2026)</ref>, nothing guarantees that a researcher's agent resembles the agents used by fraudulent participants.

text.text: Different prompts, tools, or response strategies could remove the features on which the separation depended.
Our second agent showed that this can happen: an SVM trained on one agent missed most respondents of the other (Table S5).
text.formatted: Our second agent showed that this can happen: an SVM trained on one agent missed most respondents of the other (Table <ref type="table">S5</ref>).

text.text: Our findings have practical implications for how online behavioral data are collected, evaluated, and reported.
Researchers should no longer treat valid task performance or conventional exclusion criteria as sufficient evidence of human participation.
Participant verification should become part of study design, because detection and data cleaning after collection may not be enough.
Journals and reviewers can support this by asking authors to report how human participation was verified.

Online sample providers and experiment-hosting platforms carry great responsibility, because they control infrastructure that individual researchers cannot reproduce. Gordon et al. (2026) argued that reported agent capabilities do not show actual contamination and that some platforms already screen respondents at enrollment and monitor them over time.
text.formatted: Online sample providers and experiment-hosting platforms carry great responsibility, because they control infrastructure that individual researchers cannot reproduce. <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Gordon et al. (2026)</ref> argued that reported agent capabilities do not show actual contamination and that some platforms already screen respondents at enrollment and monitor them over time.

text.text: These claims require further support.
Most existing bot-detection and authenticity checks are built into survey platforms or applied before participants enter a study (CloudResearch, n.d.; Prolific, 2026).
text.formatted: Most existing bot-detection and authenticity checks are built into survey platforms or applied before participants enter a study (CloudResearch, n.d.; <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Prolific, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: To our knowledge, as of November 2026, only one sample provider offers checks that run during a study (Prolific, 2026).
text.formatted: To our knowledge, as of November 2026, only one sample provider offers checks that run during a study <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Prolific, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: These checks work on three platforms.
Only one of them, Pavlovia, is designed to host behavioral experiments.
3   Protection during the behavioral experiment itself therefore remains largely a gap.
To illustrate this, in October 2026 the first author advertised a study on Prolific that was set up only for this test.
The AGEA (Özüdoğru, Chetverikov, et al., 2026) then took part in this study through another researcher's participant account.
text.formatted: The AGEA <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Özüdoğru, Chetverikov, et al., 2026)</ref> then took part in this study through another researcher's participant account.

text.text: 4 The AGEA completed the study undetected, without any warning or flag from Prolific.
This single test does not show how common agent participation is, but it shows that the capability can be used in practice.
3 These checks were not yet available on Pavlovia (pavlovia.org) when we collected our data, and they are still not available on Gorilla (gorilla.sc), which hosted our Stroop task.
4 The account holder consented to the use of the account.
No other participants took part, and the reward was paid only to that account.
Platforms should therefore develop participant-verification and bot-detection measures that work across experiment-hosting environments.
Independent researchers should be able to test these measures, because platforms may not disclose how they work.
These tests need to be repeated with each new generation of models, because safeguards built on current model limitations may lose their effectiveness.
Several limitations qualify these conclusions.

First, we examined one task, one hosting platform, and two agents, both developed by the first author, so we cannot say whether vulnerability or detectability depends on features of the task, although studies with other tasks suggest that the concern is broader (Özüdoğru, Chetverikov, et al., 2026; Özüdoğru, Van der Stigchel, et al., 2026).
text.formatted: First, we examined one task, one hosting platform, and two agents, both developed by the first author, so we cannot say whether vulnerability or detectability depends on features of the task, although studies with other tasks suggest that the concern is broader <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Özüdoğru, Chetverikov, et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Özüdoğru, Van der Stigchel, et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Using the Stroop task may also have made human-like data easier to produce.
It is among the most studied paradigms in psychology, so its typical results have likely entered the training data of current models.
Yet less familiar tasks are not necessarily safer.
Most new tasks build on established paradigms and share their general properties, such as right-skewed response time distributions.
To threaten online research, an agent need not reproduce every effect, only produce plausibly human data.
A second limitation concerns the online sample.
We could not verify whether its respondents were human.

It also differed from the lab sample in how it was collected, on participants' own devices and in uncontrolled environments, so differences between the online and lab samples cannot be attributed to agents alone.

In addition, the SVMs learned what human data look like from students tested in the lab, not from online participants, so they may flag online participants simply for differing from this reference sample.
A third limitation concerns the features.

Our SVMs used eight summary features of response times and task accuracy, and finer-grained features based on theoretical predictions about the task, such as effects of individual stimulus properties, may separate agents from humans better.
Finally, online sample providers and hosting platforms can also monitor other signals during data collection, such as mouse movements, keystroke timing, or browser information.
Our study addressed the case in which such checks are not in place or are not sufficient, which still applies to most behavioral experiments.
Taken together, these results show that a human-like Stroop effect no longer implies a human participant.

AI agents can produce behavioral data that pass conventional screening, and the false alarms of both SVMs and the failure of the supervised SVM to generalize to a second agent limit their usefulness for identifying agent participation in online samples.
As agentic systems improve, protecting online behavioral research will depend less on inspecting data after collection and more on verifying who produced them.
Continued tests with independently developed agents and verified online samples are needed to establish which safeguards can meet that challenge.

text.text: This supplement reports four additional analyses of the two support vector machines (SVMs) described in the main text and a completed REFORMS checklist.

The analyses test whether the results depend on the analysis choices, show which features separated the lab and artificial experiment agent (AEA) samples, test more cautious settings of the supervised SVM, and test whether the supervised SVM detects a second agent.
Several analysis choices were fixed in advance: the setting ν of the one-class SVM and the evaluation by 5,000 random splits into training and test sets.
To test whether the results depended on these choices, we varied ν and compared the main evaluation with schemes that use more data for training.
Table S1 shows the performance of the one-class SVM for values of ν from .01 to .50.

text.text: The median classifier accuracy stayed between .62 and .63 for all values, and sensitivity and specificity were the same for all values up to .30.
We collected data from 51 respondents generated by a second agent, the artificial general experiment agent (AGEA), in October 2026.

The AGEA was developed by the first author as part of a separate research project (Özüdoğru, Chetverikov, et al., 2026) and was designed to complete behavioral experiments in general rather than the Stroop task alone.

text.text: The AGEA completed the same task, and its data were processed and analyzed with the same methods as the lab and AEA data.

In each of the same 5,000 splits, one supervised SVM was trained on lab and AEA respondents and another on lab and AGEA respondents (25 of each), and both were tested on held-out lab, AEA, and AGEA respondents (26 of each).
Each SVM detected the agent it was trained on but missed most respondents of the other agent (Table S5).

text.text: The SVM trained on AEA data flagged 19% of the AGEA respondents, and the SVM trained on AGEA data flagged 35% of the AEA respondents.
Balanced accuracy fell from .94 to .54 and from .96 to .67, respectively.
It fell in every split, except for one split in which the two balanced accuracies of the SVM trained on AGEA data were tied.
Both SVMs still gave the other agent's respondents higher scores than lab respondents, but most of these scores stayed below the default decision threshold.
We did not test whether another threshold, chosen without data from the other agent, would detect it.

text.text: Figure 1The Color-Word Stroop Task
We identified eight data properties that a researcher can compute from our trial data.
These eight features were used as the input variables for both SVMs.
Mean response time and the standard deviation of response times describe how fast and how variable response times are.

Skewness of response times was included because human response time distributions have a long tail of slow responses(Heathcote et al., 1991), and a lack of this skew has been discussed as a sign of agent data(Huskey et al., 2026; Van der Stigchel et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Skewness of response times was included because human response time distributions have a long tail of slow responses<ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Heathcote et al., 1991)</ref>, and a lack of this skew has been discussed as a sign of agent data<ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Huskey et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Van der Stigchel et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Task accuracy, the proportion of correct responses, indicates whether the task was done as instructed.
Response time drift, the slope of response time across trials, was included because humans speed up with practice or slow down with fatigue during a task, whereas an agent need not.

Lag-one autocorrelation of response times was included because the response times of successive human trials are correlated(Laming, 1979), and this correlation has also been discussed as a sign of agent data(Huskey et al., 2026; Van der Stigchel et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Lag-one autocorrelation of response times was included because the response times of successive human trials are correlated<ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Laming, 1979)</ref>, and this correlation has also been discussed as a sign of agent data<ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Huskey et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Van der Stigchel et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, interference (incongruent minus neutral) and facilitation (neutral minus congruent) in mean correct response time are the two components ofthe Stroop effect (MacLeod, 1991).

The response time features used all trials with a response, so lag-one autocorrelation was computed between successive responses, including pairs separated by a missed trial or a break; task accuracy was based on all 288 trials.
The first six features can be computed for any response time task; interference and facilitation require the Stroop conditions.
We used one feature per property, because several candidate features overlapped or were derived from each other.
Figure2
Data from five lab respondents and five AEA respondents were drawn at random and shuffled as P1 to P10.
Panel a shows the distribution of correct response times and the accuracy for each condition; panel b shows the congruency effect (mean correct response time on incongruent minus congruent trials).
The x-axis in panel a ends at the 2,000 ms response deadline.
